So I don't talk about this much on here, but I have been quietly building 
something I think is actually kind of cool — a 2D physics engine where the 
classical solver trains a neural net to eventually replace the expensive parts 
of itself. The long-term goal is to get something that can run KSP or Space 
Engine scale simulations on mid-range hardware. That's the dream anyway.

Let me explain what I mean, because I feel like this gets misunderstood fast.

## What Even Is a Constraint Solver?

A classical rigid body physics engine works by defining constraints — rules 
that the simulation has to satisfy every frame. Things like "these two boxes 
cannot overlap" or "this joint has to stay connected." Every frame, the solver 
looks at all the violations and applies corrective impulses to the bodies to 
fix them. The specific method I am using is called a sequential impulse solver, 
which is what Box2D uses and what Erin Catto has been writing about for years 
in his GDC papers.[^1]

The cool thing about this approach is it is deterministic. Same inputs, same 
outputs, every time. That matters a lot for what comes next.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| fig-cap: "Every frame, in order, no exceptions."

{
  const w = 640, h = 320;
  const svg = d3.create("svg")
    .attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${w} ${h}`)
    .attr("width", "100%")
    .style("font-family", "system-ui, sans-serif");

  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  defs.append("marker")
    .attr("id", "arr")
    .attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
    .attr("refX", 8).attr("refY", 5)
    .attr("markerWidth", 6).attr("markerHeight", 6)
    .attr("orient", "auto-start-reverse")
    .append("path")
    .attr("d", "M2 1L8 5L2 9")
    .attr("fill", "none")
    .attr("stroke", "#999")
    .attr("stroke-width", 1.5)
    .attr("stroke-linecap", "round");

  const teal  = { fill: "#e1f5ee", stroke: "#0f6e56", text: "#085041" };
  const gray  = { fill: "#f1efe8", stroke: "#888780", text: "#444441" };

  function box(g, x, y, bw, bh, color, title, sub) {
    g.append("rect")
      .attr("x", x).attr("y", y).attr("width", bw).attr("height", bh)
      .attr("rx", 8).attr("fill", color.fill)
      .attr("stroke", color.stroke).attr("stroke-width", 0.5);
    if (sub) {
      g.append("text").attr("x", x+bw/2).attr("y", y+bh/2-9)
        .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("dominant-baseline","central")
        .attr("fill", color.text).attr("font-size", 13).attr("font-weight", 500)
        .text(title);
      g.append("text").attr("x", x+bw/2).attr("y", y+bh/2+10)
        .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("dominant-baseline","central")
        .attr("fill", color.stroke).attr("font-size", 11).text(sub);
    } else {
      g.append("text").attr("x", x+bw/2).attr("y", y+bh/2)
        .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("dominant-baseline","central")
        .attr("fill", color.text).attr("font-size", 13).attr("font-weight", 500)
        .text(title);
    }
  }

  function arrow(g, x1, y1, x2, y2) {
    g.append("line")
      .attr("x1",x1).attr("y1",y1).attr("x2",x2).attr("y2",y2)
      .attr("stroke","#bbb").attr("stroke-width",1.2)
      .attr("marker-end","url(#arr)");
  }

  const root = svg.append("g");

  box(root, 240, 20, 160, 44, gray, "Game loop", null);
  arrow(root, 320, 64, 320, 94);
  root.append("text").attr("x",335).attr("y",83)
    .attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#bbb").text("dt = 1/60s");

  const steps = [
    { y:94,  title:"Integrate forces",      sub:"Semi-implicit Euler, gravity",    ms:"~0.2ms" },
    { y:178, title:"Broadphase",            sub:"AABB overlap, O(n²) for now",     ms:"~0.5ms" },
    { y:262, title:"Narrowphase + resolve", sub:"SAT, sequential impulse solver",  ms:"~2-8ms" },
  ];

  steps.forEach((s, i) => {
    box(root, 200, s.y, 240, 54, teal, s.title, s.sub);
    if (i < steps.length - 1) arrow(root, 320, s.y+54, 320, s.y+84);
    root.append("text").attr("x",60).attr("y",s.y+27)
      .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#bbb").text(s.ms);
  });

  root.append("text").attr("x",60).attr("y",42)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#bbb")
    .text("budget: 16.6ms");

  root.append("path")
    .attr("d","M440 289 L540 289 L540 42 L400 42")
    .attr("fill","none").attr("stroke","#ccc")
    .attr("stroke-width",1).attr("stroke-dasharray","5 4")
    .attr("marker-end","url(#arr)");

  root.append("text").attr("x",554).attr("y",170)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#bbb")
    .attr("transform","rotate(-90 554 170)").text("next frame");

  return svg.node();
}
```

## So Where Does the ML Come In?

Here is the thing — constraint solvers scale badly. The more bodies you have, 
the more constraints you have, the more work the solver has to do every frame. 
KSP2 is a great example of this going wrong. Every part of every vessel is 
running through a full constraint solve every frame, and the game runs like 
garbage on anything but high end hardware.

The idea I am working with is: similar physical configurations tend to produce 
similar outcomes. A stack of boxes falling looks basically the same whether it's 
these three boxes or those three boxes. A neural net can learn to recognize 
those patterns and predict what the solver would have done — without actually 
running the solver.

So the pipeline is basically:

1. Run the classical solver on a bunch of random scenarios
2. Record every `(state before step, state after step)` pair
3. Train a small neural net to learn that mapping
4. At runtime, route "boring" or "familiar" physics through the net, 
   and fall back to the real solver for anything complex or novel

The thing that makes this actually viable is that **the solver generates its 
own training data**. I don't need a dataset. I just need to run the engine.[^2]

Drag the slider. Find where your game breaks.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bodyCount = Inputs.range([10, 250], {
  value: 80, step: 1, label: "Bodies in scene"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const n = bodyCount;
  const frames = Array.from({length:25}, (_,i) => (i+1)*10);
  const solverMs = frames.map(b => +(b*b*0.002 + b*0.02).toFixed(1));
  const overBudget = (+(n*n*0.002 + n*0.02).toFixed(1)) > 16.6;
  const solverAtN = +(n*n*0.002 + n*0.02).toFixed(1);

  const w=640, h=280, mL=55, mR=20, mT=24, mB=40;
  const iW=w-mL-mR, iH=h-mT-mB;
  const xS = d3.scaleLinear([10,250],[0,iW]);
  const yS = d3.scaleLinear([0,130],[iH,0]);

  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox",`0 0 ${w} ${h}`)
    .attr("width","100%").style("font-family","system-ui, sans-serif");
  const g = svg.append("g").attr("transform",`translate(${mL},${mT})`);

  yS.ticks(5).forEach(t => {
    g.append("line").attr("x1",0).attr("x2",iW)
      .attr("y1",yS(t)).attr("y2",yS(t))
      .attr("stroke","#e5e5e3").attr("stroke-width",1);
  });

  g.append("line").attr("x1",0).attr("x2",iW)
    .attr("y1",yS(16.6)).attr("y2",yS(16.6))
    .attr("stroke","#e24b4a").attr("stroke-width",1.5)
    .attr("stroke-dasharray","6 4");
  g.append("text").attr("x",iW-4).attr("y",yS(16.6)-5)
    .attr("text-anchor","end").attr("font-size",10).attr("fill","#e24b4a")
    .text("16.6ms budget");

  g.append("path")
    .datum(frames.map((f,i)=>[f,0.8]))
    .attr("fill","rgba(27,175,122,0.08)")
    .attr("d", d3.area().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y0(iH).y1(d=>yS(d[1])));
  g.append("path")
    .datum(frames.map((f,i)=>[f,0.8]))
    .attr("fill","none").attr("stroke","#1baf7a").attr("stroke-width",2)
    .attr("d", d3.line().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y(d=>yS(d[1])));

  g.append("path")
    .datum(frames.map((f,i)=>[f,solverMs[i]]))
    .attr("fill","rgba(42,120,214,0.08)")
    .attr("d", d3.area().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y0(iH).y1(d=>yS(Math.min(d[1],130))));
  g.append("path")
    .datum(frames.map((f,i)=>[f,solverMs[i]]))
    .attr("fill","none").attr("stroke","#2a78d6").attr("stroke-width",2)
    .attr("d", d3.line().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y(d=>yS(Math.min(d[1],130))));

  g.append("line")
    .attr("x1",xS(n)).attr("x2",xS(n)).attr("y1",0).attr("y2",iH)
    .attr("stroke", overBudget ? "#e24b4a" : "#999")
    .attr("stroke-width",1).attr("stroke-dasharray","4 3");
  g.append("circle")
    .attr("cx",xS(n)).attr("cy",yS(Math.min(solverAtN,128)))
    .attr("r",5).attr("fill", overBudget ? "#e24b4a" : "#2a78d6");
  g.append("text")
    .attr("x",xS(n)+6).attr("y",yS(Math.min(solverAtN,125))-6)
    .attr("font-size",10).attr("fill", overBudget ? "#e24b4a" : "#2a78d6")
    .text(`${n} bodies → ${solverAtN}ms${overBudget ? " ⚠ over budget" : ""}`);

  g.append("g").attr("transform",`translate(0,${iH})`)
    .call(d3.axisBottom(xS).ticks(8))
    .selectAll("text").attr("fill","#898781").attr("font-size",10);
  g.append("g")
    .call(d3.axisLeft(yS).ticks(5).tickFormat(d=>d+"ms"))
    .selectAll("text").attr("fill","#898781").attr("font-size",10);

  g.append("text").attr("x",iW/2).attr("y",iH+34)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#898781")
    .text("Bodies in scene");
  g.append("text").attr("transform","rotate(-90)")
    .attr("x",-iH/2).attr("y",-42)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#898781")
    .text("Frame time (ms)");

  const leg = svg.append("g").attr("transform",`translate(${mL},8)`);
  [["#2a78d6","Classical solver O(n²)"],["#1baf7a","Neural approximator"],["#e24b4a","Frame budget"]].forEach(([c,l],i)=>{
    leg.append("rect").attr("x",i*180).attr("y",0).attr("width",10).attr("height",10).attr("rx",2).attr("fill",c);
    leg.append("text").attr("x",i*180+14).attr("y",9).attr("font-size",10).attr("fill","#666").text(l);
  });

  return svg.node();
}
```

## Where It's At Right Now

The 2D engine is built in C++ using xmake — broadphase collision detection, 
SAT narrowphase for circles and boxes, sequential impulse resolution, the whole 
thing. It runs a multithreaded data generator that spins up one physics world 
per CPU thread, runs random scenarios, and writes binary files that Python can 
read for training.

The neural net itself is a small residual MLP — predicts the *change* in state 
rather than the absolute state, which keeps the outputs small and makes training 
way more stable. About 531k parameters, which is nothing. Runs in under a 
millisecond on any modern GPU.

I am still in early days — first real training run hasn't finished yet — but 
the pipeline is working end to end. TensorBoard is logging everything including 
side-by-side videos of what the solver does vs what the net predicts, so I can 
actually see where it diverges.[^3]

## Why 2D First?

Honestly, 2D is just a proving ground. The goal is 3D, targeting RTX 30x0 as 
the minimum. But 3D introduces a bunch of problems that 2D doesn't have — 
rotation alone gets way more complicated (quaternions are annoying for neural 
nets, there's actually a whole paper on this[^4]), and contact geometry becomes 
dramatically harder.

The 2D engine gives me a working data pipeline I can trust, training 
infrastructure I know works, and something to write about while the harder 
stuff is being figured out. Also it's just easier to debug when you can see 
everything in a flat 2D view.

## What's Next

Getting the first training run done and looking at rollout stability — that's 
the real metric that matters. A 1% position error per frame sounds small until 
you realize it compounds into garbage after about two seconds of simulation. The 
question is how many frames the net can run unassisted before it needs a 
correction from the real solver.

Drag the slider. See how fast it falls apart.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof errorPct = Inputs.range([0.2, 3.0], {
  value: 1.0, step: 0.1, label: "Per-frame error rate (%)"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const FRAMES=300, THRESH=0.5;
  const rate = errorPct/100;
  const fl = Array.from({length:FRAMES},(_,i)=>i);
  const rollout = fl.map(i => Math.min(Math.pow(1+rate,i)-1, 8));
  const divF = rollout.findIndex(v=>v>=THRESH);

  const w=640,h=260,mL=55,mR=20,mT=24,mB=40;
  const iW=w-mL-mR, iH=h-mT-mB;
  const xS=d3.scaleLinear([0,FRAMES],[0,iW]);
  const yS=d3.scaleLinear([0,4],[iH,0]);

  const svg=d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox",`0 0 ${w} ${h}`)
    .attr("width","100%").style("font-family","system-ui, sans-serif");
  const g=svg.append("g").attr("transform",`translate(${mL},${mT})`);

  yS.ticks(4).forEach(t=>{
    g.append("line").attr("x1",0).attr("x2",iW)
      .attr("y1",yS(t)).attr("y2",yS(t))
      .attr("stroke","#e5e5e3").attr("stroke-width",1);
  });

  [60,120,180,240,300].forEach(f=>{
    g.append("text").attr("x",xS(f)).attr("y",iH+28)
      .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",9).attr("fill","#bbb")
      .text(`${f/60}s`);
  });

  g.append("line").attr("x1",0).attr("x2",iW)
    .attr("y1",yS(THRESH)).attr("y2",yS(THRESH))
    .attr("stroke","#e24b4a").attr("stroke-width",1.5)
    .attr("stroke-dasharray","6 4");
  g.append("text").attr("x",iW-4).attr("y",yS(THRESH)-5)
    .attr("text-anchor","end").attr("font-size",10).attr("fill","#e24b4a")
    .text("visible divergence");

  g.append("line").attr("x1",0).attr("x2",iW)
    .attr("y1",yS(0)).attr("y2",yS(0))
    .attr("stroke","#2a78d6").attr("stroke-width",2);

  g.append("path")
    .datum(fl.map((f,i)=>[f,rollout[i]]))
    .attr("fill","rgba(237,161,0,0.1)")
    .attr("d",d3.area().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y0(iH).y1(d=>yS(Math.min(d[1],4))));
  g.append("path")
    .datum(fl.map((f,i)=>[f,rollout[i]]))
    .attr("fill","none").attr("stroke","#eda100").attr("stroke-width",2)
    .attr("d",d3.line().x(d=>xS(d[0])).y(d=>yS(Math.min(d[1],4))).curve(d3.curveBasis));

  if (divF>=0 && divF<FRAMES) {
    g.append("line")
      .attr("x1",xS(divF)).attr("x2",xS(divF)).attr("y1",0).attr("y2",iH)
      .attr("stroke","#e24b4a").attr("stroke-width",1).attr("stroke-dasharray","4 3");
    g.append("text").attr("x",xS(divF)+4).attr("y",14)
      .attr("font-size",10).attr("fill","#e24b4a")
      .text(`diverges at frame ${divF} (${(divF/60).toFixed(1)}s)`);
  }

  g.append("g").attr("transform",`translate(0,${iH})`)
    .call(d3.axisBottom(xS).ticks(6).tickFormat(d=>`f${d}`))
    .selectAll("text").attr("fill","#898781").attr("font-size",10);
  g.append("g")
    .call(d3.axisLeft(yS).ticks(4).tickFormat(d=>d.toFixed(1)+"m"))
    .selectAll("text").attr("fill","#898781").attr("font-size",10);

  g.append("text").attr("x",iW/2).attr("y",iH+36)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#898781")
    .text("Frames (60fps)");
  g.append("text").attr("transform","rotate(-90)")
    .attr("x",-iH/2).attr("y",-42)
    .attr("text-anchor","middle").attr("font-size",11).attr("fill","#898781")
    .text("Position error (m)");

  const leg=svg.append("g").attr("transform",`translate(${mL},8)`);
  [["#2a78d6","Ground truth (solver)"],["#eda100","Neural rollout error"],["#e24b4a","Visible threshold"]].forEach(([c,l],i)=>{
    leg.append("rect").attr("x",i*185).attr("y",0).attr("width",10).attr("height",10).attr("rx",2).attr("fill",c);
    leg.append("text").attr("x",i*185+14).attr("y",9).attr("font-size",10).attr("fill","#666").text(l);
  });

  return svg.node();
}
```

After that, the arbiter — the piece that decides which path each object takes 
per frame. That's where the interesting engineering is.

3D is the end goal. Steam Deck support after that, maybe.

[^1]: Catto's GDC papers are genuinely some of the best technical writing in 
gamedev. https://box2d.org/publications/

[^2]: This is also kind of what the paper "Learning to Simulate Complex Physics 
with Graph Networks" (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., ICML 2020) does, except they use 
graph neural nets and I am using a plain MLP. https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.09405

[^3]: The video logging runs in a background thread so it doesn't block the GPU 
during training. Small thing but it matters.

[^4]: "On the Continuity of Rotation Representations in Neural Networks" — Zhou 
et al., CVPR 2019. Short version: don't use naive quaternion MSE loss, it breaks. 
https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.07035
